scene.testo: After 340 days in orbit, one astronaut stood up on Earth and almost collapsed. Her body weighed what it always had, but it felt like carrying a refrigerator. Today, you find out why coming home hurts so much.
Imagine you are strapped into a cramped capsule, 250 miles above Earth. For months, you floated freely. Now your body is about to face the planet again. Every muscle you own is about to be tested.

The station looks peaceful behind you, flying at 17,500 miles per hour. It circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes. You have lived here for months. In a few hours, you will be standing on solid ground.

First comes goodbye. The crew staying behind floats beside you, hugging, smiling, filming. Hatches must be sealed with care. Once the capsule separates, there is no going back. Home is waiting, and it will not be gentle.
Before leaving, you put on a special suit. It is tight around your legs on purpose. Its job is to push blood downward, because your body forgot how to handle gravity after months of floating.

In space, fluids in your body shift toward your head. Your face puffs up. Your legs get thinner. Astronauts have joked about having bird legs and chubby cheeks. It is a real, documented effect of microgravity.

Now the capsule undocks. Small thrusters push you gently away from the station. The first moments are calm, almost quiet. Then the engine fires for about four minutes, slowing you down so Earth can pull you in.
The capsule has three parts. Only the middle one carries you home. The other two will burn up in the atmosphere. In the little cabin, you sit in a custom seat molded to fit your body exactly.
Then comes the fire. Reentry begins around 75 miles above the ground. The capsule hits the air at about 17,000 miles per hour. Air in front of it compresses and glows hotter than a furnace.
Outside your window, orange flames lick the glass. Temperatures on the heat shield can reach roughly 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit. That is hot enough to melt steel. Inside, you hold your breath and wait.

Then the weight arrives. You feel it crushing your chest. During a Soyuz descent, astronauts can experience around four to five times Earth's gravity. Your arms feel like lead. Breathing becomes a struggle.
Remember, you have not felt weight for months. Suddenly your body is thousands of pounds heavy. If you weigh 170 pounds, it can feel like carrying a grand piano sitting on your chest for minutes.

At about six miles up, the parachute deploys. A small pilot chute pulls out the main one. The jolt shakes you hard. The main canopy covers roughly 3,000 square feet, about the size of a basketball court.

Slowly, the capsule swings under the huge canopy. The ride becomes strangely calm after the fire. Your speed drops from thousands of miles per hour to something survivable. But the hardest moment is still coming.
About three feet above the ground, small engines fire. They are called soft landing rockets. Even so, the landing is a hard hit. Astronauts often describe it as a car crash you walk away from.
The capsule slams into the Kazakhstan steppe, then often tips on its side. Dust swirls. Silence follows. You are home, hanging in your seat, and for the first time in months, gravity owns you.
Rescue teams race toward you in helicopters and trucks. They reach the capsule within minutes. Doors open. Cold air rushes in. For the first time in months, you smell real Earth air, grass and dust.

You try to lift your arm. It feels impossible. Your head feels like a bowling ball. Even holding a pen is a struggle. After long missions, astronauts say the first minutes feel like extreme exhaustion.
Recovery crews lift you out and place you in a chair. Yes, you get carried. Your balance system, the inner ear, has not worked normally for months. Standing up could make the whole world spin.

Many returning astronauts feel dizzy and nauseous. Some vomit within minutes. Your brain is confused, trying to relearn which way is down. Doctors are standing by, checking your pulse, blood pressure and eyes.

A tent is set up nearby for quick medical exams. Astronauts are also given a phone call to family. Cameras are everywhere. But your body wants one thing: rest. Walking is not allowed for the first hour.

Why is it so hard? In space, your muscles barely work. Everything floats. Without gravity, bones lose density. On long missions, astronauts can lose about one percent of bone mass every month in some areas.

That is why astronauts exercise about two hours every day. They run on a treadmill, strapped down by a harness. They lift weights using a special machine. Even so, their bodies still weaken during long missions.

Your heart changes too. In orbit it does not have to fight gravity, so it can become slightly rounder. Blood vessels adapt. When you return, standing up can make you faint because blood pools in your legs.

Your eyes can change as well. Some astronauts on long missions develop vision problems because of fluid shifting toward the head. NASA has studied this for years and still investigates its exact causes.

Your skin is different too. After months without walking, the soles of your feet become soft and thin. When you finally stand, astronauts have described the feeling like walking on hot coals or sharp pebbles.

Now imagine your first walk. Your legs shake. Your balance fails. Doctors hold your arms on both sides. Astronauts say gravity feels like wearing a heavy backpack filled with wet sand, all day, everywhere.
A flight surgeon will check you again within hours. Then you fly to Houston or another medical base. It is a long trip. During the flight, you must stay hydrated and keep your legs moving.

At the Johnson Space Center, rehabilitation begins. NASA gives returning astronauts a program that can last 45 days. It includes stretching, strength training, balance work and walking. Recovery is a full-time job.
scene.q: astronaut rehabilitation exercise Johnson Space Center

scene.testo: Trainers help you rebuild everything. You balance on foam pads. You walk in straight lines with your eyes closed. Even small tasks, like turning your head quickly, can make you dizzy for the first days.

Bone recovery takes much longer than muscle recovery. Studies of long-duration crew members suggest some bone loss may not fully return, even a year after landing. Scientists are still studying how much comes back.

Meanwhile, your brain is relearning. In space, you push off walls with a fingertip. On Earth, you drop things constantly. Astronauts report letting go of objects, expecting them to float, and watching them crash to the floor.

That habit is real. Returning crew members have described reaching for something, letting go, and being surprised when it fell. It usually fades within days. But it shows how deeply space rewires your instincts.
Sleep changes as well. On the station, you sleep in a bag attached to a wall. No pillow. No mattress. Back on Earth, a soft bed feels strange, and many astronauts say it takes days to adjust.

Food changes too. In orbit, taste is dulled because fluids shift to your head, which makes you feel stuffy. Astronauts often crave spicy sauces. Back on Earth, many describe fresh fruit as an overwhelming explosion of flavor.

Smells hit hard as well. After months of recycled air, a forest, rain or even a rainy parking lot can be overwhelming. Several astronauts have written about how amazing nature smells right after landing.
scene.q: astronaut outdoors fresh air after landing

scene.testo: Then there is the view. From orbit, you watched about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day. Now you get one of each. Many astronauts say the sky looks strangely small after living above it.

Some astronauts describe a feeling called the overview effect. Looking at Earth from above, borders disappear. The atmosphere looks paper thin. Returning home, many say they see our planet with new, deeper appreciation.

And yes, there is a cost. Radiation is one. On the station, astronauts absorb far more radiation than people on the ground. NASA tracks every crew member's dose carefully, and sets career limits to protect their health.

A famous example is the twins study. NASA compared an astronaut who spent nearly a year in orbit with his identical twin on Earth. Researchers found changes in gene expression, which mostly returned to normal after landing.

Some changes did seem to persist. The study noted small shifts in thinking speed and accuracy after return. NASA stresses that the results come from just one pair of twins, so conclusions remain limited.

After weeks, life slowly feels normal. Muscles return. Balance stabilizes. Astronauts walk again without help, drive again, and hug their families without thinking. But the memory of floating never fully leaves them.
Many say they dream of flying. Some wake up reaching for the ceiling. Others say they miss the silence of orbit, the quiet hum of fans, and the endless blue view below their feet.

Now compare it with life on Earth. You walk to the kitchen, open the fridge and pour a glass of water. In orbit, that simple glass would float away as a wobbling sphere. Gravity makes everything feel simple.

Here is the most surprising detail. After months in orbit, some astronauts say the first thing they notice is weight itself. Not the big stuff. A single cup of coffee, held in a hand, feels strangely heavy.

That is the secret of coming home. Gravity is not just a force. It is something your body forgets and must relearn. And every astronaut who returns discovers that simply standing up is an achievement.

descrizione:
What happens when an astronaut finally comes back to Earth? After months in orbit, the return trip is a violent, exhausting and surprising experience. In this Orbital Days documentary, you ride along with a Soyuz crew from undocking at the International Space Station to the hard landing in Kazakhstan, and then follow the long road to recovery.

Discover how reentry heat, four to five times Earth's gravity, bone loss, balance problems and NASA rehabilitation shape the astronaut experience. We explain the science of microgravity, the twins study, and why even a cup of coffee can feel heavy after months of floating.

All facts come from documented NASA and ESA sources and astronauts' own accounts. Where something is uncertain, we say so. Subscribe to Orbital Days for more stories about real life in space.
